candidate-40: The difference is an excellent reminder that names can be transmitted in forms that resemble other biblical names. It affects the wording of Matthew’s genealogy without changing its sequence from David to the exile.
candidate-41: The location label changes, but the encounter, the two possessed men, and Jesus’ authority remain the same. Readers should distinguish a geographical textual question from the separate Synoptic question of how Matthew’s account relates to Mark and Luke.
candidate-42: The verse supplies the report that prompts Jesus’ reply, but the surrounding narrative still makes the waiting family clear. A missing verse number here is not a missing teaching and should not be turned into a claim about motive.
candidate-43: The longer form gives Jesus’ rebuke a memorable weather analogy; the shorter form moves directly to the demand for a sign. The comparison is especially useful because a familiar saying may be bracketed or footnoted even when every edition displayed in the app prints it.
candidate-44: The additional clause extends the explicit adultery warning to the man marrying a divorced woman. The main prohibition and its exception remain in every displayed edition, so teaching should identify the added application precisely rather than implying that the whole verse is disputed.
candidate-45: Both forms make the obedient son the one who initially refuses and later acts, but they assign that behavior to a differently ordered son. The moral contrast survives while the dialogue and answer visibly change.
candidate-46: The phrase raises an immediate Christological question because it explicitly includes the Son among those who do not know the day or hour. Its presence should be interpreted within Matthew’s whole presentation of the Son, not used alone either to deny Christ’s divinity or to dissolve the plain force of the saying.
candidate-47: If the prisoner is called Jesus Barabbas, Pilate’s choice is verbally sharper: Jesus Barabbas or Jesus called Christ. The alternative does not change which prisoner is released, but it changes the rhetoric of the scene.
candidate-48: The added sentence would place the piercing before Jesus’ death in Matthew, while John narrates a spear thrust after death. Because none of the displayed editions contains it, the article must present it as a reported alternative rather than as a demonstrated edition reading.
candidate-49: Compassion and anger produce very different first impressions of Jesus’ response to the leper, even though both lead to the same touch and healing. The emotional term therefore merits attention without inviting an unsupported story about why a scribe changed it.
candidate-50: The longer form repeats a judgment saying known from the mission discourse in Matthew. Its absence does not remove Jesus’ command about shaking off the dust or the warning carried by that act.
candidate-51: Calling Jesus the carpenter emphasizes his own trade; calling him the carpenter’s son emphasizes family identification. Either reading belongs to the same scene of hometown familiarity and offense.
candidate-52: The difference affects an ascetic practice attached to the disciples’ failure, but every edition still places the emphasis on dependence expressed in prayer. It should not be used to disparage either prayer or fasting.
candidate-53: The unqualified form makes entry into God’s kingdom difficult in itself; the expanded form explicitly locates the difficulty in trusting wealth. The verses immediately following continue to speak about riches and God’s power in every edition.
candidate-54: The difference changes the grammar of the angelic proclamation rather than its central announcement of glory to God and peace on earth. It is a classic case where one letter can materially influence an English rendering.
candidate-55: Naming Joseph avoids calling him Jesus’ father, while the critical form describes him according to his social and family role in the scene. Neither wording overturns Luke’s preceding account of Jesus’ conception.
candidate-56: The longer form completes the familiar quotation from Deuteronomy, while the shorter form preserves only the answer about bread. Both forms present Jesus resisting temptation through Scripture.
candidate-57: Chosen and beloved are both titles of divine approval, but they connect the Transfiguration voice to different wording and biblical echoes. The command to listen to Jesus remains unchanged.
candidate-58: The expansion states both a rebuke about the disciples’ spirit and a saving purpose for the Son of Man. The shorter text still records Jesus rebuking them and refusing the destructive proposal, so the narrative judgment is not erased.
candidate-59: Seventy and seventy-two may evoke somewhat different biblical number patterns, but the mission, instructions, and return are the same. Counts should be reported by named edition rather than harmonized silently.
candidate-60: The shorter form would remove much of Luke’s explicit cup-and-covenant wording at this point. Because the displayed editions all print the longer form, the article must keep the reported manuscript alternative separate from their shared text.
candidate-61: The alternatives differ in how the criminal addresses Jesus, not in the request to be remembered or Jesus’ promise of paradise. The passage’s confession and comfort remain recognizable in either form.
candidate-62: Double brackets are an editorial signal, not an erasure. The bodily demonstration fits the surrounding insistence that the risen Jesus is not a disembodied spirit, which remains explicit in the neighboring verses.
candidate-63: Son of God and Chosen One are different titles with different echoes, though both identify Jesus as uniquely appointed by God. Since the app’s editions agree, the alternative must remain tied to the exact publisher note until fuller evidence is reviewed.
candidate-64: The added clause explicitly describes the Son of Man as being in heaven while speaking on earth. Its absence shortens the saying but does not remove the descent-and-ascent contrast already present in the verse.
candidate-65: The longer Byzantine/TR form combines Messiah and divine-sonship titles; the critical form uses the distinctive title Holy One of God. Both are confessional readings, so the difference should not be framed as belief versus unbelief.
candidate-66: Without yet, Jesus’ later journey can sound like a contradiction of his statement; with yet, the temporal qualification is explicit. The surrounding narrative and the possibility of a private rather than public journey still require careful reading.
candidate-67: Son of Man connects the question to a major Johannine title; Son of God makes the confession more directly explicit. The healed man’s movement toward worship continues in either form.
candidate-68: The grammatical alternatives affect whether the emphasis falls on the Father’s gift or on the Father himself as greater than all. Every form continues into the security claim that no one can snatch the sheep from the Father’s hand.
candidate-69: The explicit me makes Jesus the direct recipient of the prayer or request; its omission leaves the construction less explicit. The promise that Jesus will act remains present in every displayed edition.
candidate-70: Present and future forms place different temporal emphasis on the Spirit’s relation to the disciples. The wider discourse still speaks both of the Spirit’s present presence and the promised coming.
candidate-71: The expansion imports sayings familiar from Paul’s later retellings and gives Saul an additional question before entering Damascus. All displayed forms retain the confrontation with the risen Jesus and Saul’s commissioning trajectory.
candidate-72: Greeks points naturally to Gentile hearers, while Hellenists can refer to Greek-speaking Jews. The difference therefore affects how readers date the Antioch mission’s crossing of an ethnic boundary.
candidate-73: To and from Jerusalem point in opposite directions and affect how the travel notice is connected to the relief visit. The travelers and completed ministry remain the same.
candidate-74: The quoted words are the same, while the psalm’s ordinal number differs. The case illustrates how headings and numbering can vary without changing the quotation itself.
candidate-75: Spirit of Jesus makes the Christological identification explicit; Spirit alone relies on the surrounding context. In both readings divine guidance redirects the missionaries toward Macedonia.
candidate-76: Me makes Paul’s statement autobiographical; you applies it directly to the addressees. The liberation remains located in Christ Jesus and opposed to sin and death.
candidate-77: One form explicitly names God as the acting subject, while the other can sound as though circumstances work by themselves. The following clause about those called according to God’s purpose anchors both readings in divine agency.
candidate-78: Word of Christ may mean the message about or from Christ; word of God names the source more generally. Either reading connects faith with hearing the proclaimed message.
candidate-79: God and Christ identify the judgment seat differently, but the following quotation and conclusion place universal confession and accountability before God. The difference should be explained without constructing rival doctrines of judgment.
candidate-80: Testimony emphasizes Paul’s proclamation; mystery emphasizes the divine content once hidden and now announced. Since the displayed editions agree on testimony, the other reading must be presented through the publisher note only.
candidate-81: The added clause extends bodily glorification to the human spirit and adds an ownership statement. The shorter text still grounds bodily holiness in belonging to God.
candidate-82: Christ explicitly identifies the wilderness figure; Lord uses the title found in the scriptural narrative. Both readings warn the Corinthian church through Israel’s example.
candidate-83: Broken gives the bread saying a vivid sacrificial description, while the shorter form says simply that the body is for you. The command to remember Christ and the cup saying continue to interpret the meal in every edition.
candidate-84: Relocating the verses after verse 40 changes their relation to the surrounding instructions but does not remove them. This makes the passage an important example of placement variation rather than simple inclusion or omission.
candidate-85: The future form promises that believers will bear the heavenly image; the exhortation calls them to do so. The contrast between the earthly and heavenly figures remains the framework for both.
candidate-86: The alternatives rearrange the relation between dying and transformation at the resurrection. Paul’s declaration of a mystery and the final victory over death remain intact.
candidate-87: Holiness describes conduct set apart before God; simplicity stresses sincerity or singleness. Both readings place Paul’s confidence in divine grace rather than worldly wisdom.
candidate-88: The longer list names adultery separately before sexual immorality; the shorter list begins with the broader term. Sexual sin remains among the works of the flesh in either form.
candidate-89: Without in Ephesus, the opening can read like a more general or circulating address; with it, the destination is explicit. That question concerns the letter’s address, not whether the letter belongs in the New Testament.
candidate-90: Word of God explicitly names the message’s source; word alone relies on the surrounding gospel context. The point that Paul’s imprisonment emboldened others remains unchanged.
candidate-91: Seen and not seen reverse the surface description of the visionary person’s claimed experience. The warning against self-inflation and detachment from the Head remains the controlling context.
candidate-92: From the beginning emphasizes the time or priority of God’s choice; firstfruits describes the believers’ representative place in a larger harvest. Both readings attribute salvation to God’s choosing work through sanctification and faith.
candidate-93: The divine title changes, but Timothy is still charged to warn against ruinous word-battles in the presence of divine authority. The unit is useful for showing how a one-word variant can alter reference without altering the exhortation.
candidate-94: The longer form piles up closely related qualities for teaching; the shorter form names integrity and dignity without the additional term. The pastoral demand for exemplary conduct remains the same.
candidate-95: In us includes Paul and his companions in the acknowledged good; in you directs the phrase toward Philemon or the recipients. The difference affects the prayer’s interpersonal emphasis, not its goal of effective fellowship in Christ.
candidate-96: Prisoners broadens the sympathy to an afflicted group; my chains makes the connection personal to the writer. The second difference, in heaven, makes the location of the better possession explicit without changing its permanence.
candidate-97: The grammatical forms support different accounts of what was not joined to faith: the message or the hearers. Both readings explain why hearing good news did not benefit the wilderness generation.
candidate-98: The variants affect whether Sarah is straightforwardly the grammatical subject and whether giving birth is stated explicitly. Every displayed form presents the fulfillment as grounded in confidence in the faithful Promiser.
candidate-99: The feminine-only address invokes the prophetic image of covenant infidelity; the expanded form makes the rebuke explicitly inclusive. Friendship with the world remains enmity with God in every edition.
candidate-100: Into salvation states the goal of growth explicitly; the shorter form leaves the goal unstated. The call to crave pure spiritual milk remains unchanged.
candidate-101: Christ as Lord directly applies Isaiah’s language to Christ; Lord God follows the wording familiar from the scriptural source. Both readings call believers to holy fear and readiness to answer for their hope.
candidate-102: The pronouns shift responsibility between the writers and the recipients: what we or you worked for, and what we or you may receive. The warning to guard the fruit of faithful labor remains clear.
candidate-103: The forms differ over whether Jude names two or three groups and over which receive mercy or rescue with fear. The pastoral movement from mercy to urgent rescue remains, but its exact arrangement changes.
candidate-104: The alternative number materially changes attempts to identify the beast by calculation, though it does not change the passage’s call for wisdom. Because all displayed editions read 666, the article must not make the manuscript alternative look like a displayed edition reading.
